u1:
The vaccination point belongs here. It's one of the values that would decide whether I could raise children inside a community at all. I'm not trying to design a village for everyone. A community needs enough agreement on children's health that parents can actually trust one another.

The grown child's review matters more than founders usually want it to. Adults can describe their intentions forever. The person who lived through the system may eventually describe something else.
u2:
A friend who reviewed this draft grew up in a Christian commune in Colorado, where her father was a pastor. She calls her childhood “a treasure and a burden.” The treasure was belonging, and having everybody care for everybody. The burden was a strict religious life she never chose.

That sentence is more useful than another promotional video of smiling children carrying vegetables.
u3:
My position is that mothers raise their own children, inside a community where the care really is shared. The village can take on meals, supervision, teaching, protection, play, and a lot of the fathering. It should never take a child away from the mother in the name of liberating her.

Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept is one of the biggest reasons I think community matters for children. Her account of the Ye'kuana is one outsider's interpretation, and she may idealize what she saw. But the picture is still powerful. Babies are carried inside ordinary adult life. Children are surrounded by people of several ages, and they learn by taking part. And one exhausted parent isn't expected to become the child's whole social world. A nuclear household can imitate pieces of this. A real village can make it normal.
u4:
Experiments where children sleep and live apart from their parents need special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that communal sleeping eventually ended, through a mix of developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. High-quality group care, and several loving adults, can be good for children. Replacing a secure attachment to the parents is a different matter.

Tamera's Children's Place deserves to be studied directly, not caricatured. My own bias is still toward systems that widen a child's circle without making the bond between parent and child ideologically inconvenient.
u5:
Children also need some territory that belongs to them. Places where they can build their own society of children, make up games, sort out ordinary disputes, and get some freedom from constant adult management.

I got a taste of that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it's still one of the freest memories I have. ZEGG's Kinderhaus works from a similar idea. The adults hold the outer safety, and the children still get a world of their own.
u6:
This can be badly misunderstood, so the safeguards have to be spelled out. A children's territory can't turn into a place where adults stop paying attention. Or where older kids dominate younger ones without anyone noticing. Or where secrecy gets treated as independence.

I also reject the suburban panic that treats every warm relationship between a child and an unrelated adult as suspicious. Children do well with lots of adults around who know them and enjoy them, who notice when something changes, and who will act when something's wrong. Fear can destroy that gift without actually preventing abuse.
u7:
The protection has several parts:

Give children real agency. Their “no” matters. No adult is entitled to a child's affection, physical contact, obedience beyond what legitimate safety requires, or private access.

Make a no-secrets rule. No adult asks a child to hide a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation, or a relationship from the child's mother or another trusted adult. A surprise has a date when it ends. Secrets meant to isolate the child are forbidden.
u8:
Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. Children should understand that their words carry power, and that adults will take them seriously. That teaching must never turn into interrogation, into punishing a child for being unsure, or into a reason to dismiss what a child reports. A scared or confused child may tell the story imperfectly and still need protecting.

Hear the child even when the accused person is someone people love. This is where communities fail, because that adult may be charismatic, useful, wealthy, spiritually important, or everybody's friend. Decide how you'll respond before anyone's face is attached to it. Immediate safety comes first. The investigation has to be competent and fair. And nobody's status buys silence.
u9: Keep relationships, and a way to report, outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give children perspective, and somewhere to speak. At least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route should be reachable without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 children in the Island Pond raid, and the court gave them back after it rejected the state's blanket request. State intervention can fail spectacularly. A community that closes itself off completely can fail too. Children need more than one world.
u10: I also searched the research corpus for a well-documented case, in an intentional community, of a child who stayed seriously dangerous to other people, where the record follows the whole sequence: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened afterwards. I didn't find one. That may be because the records are private, or because cases were sent elsewhere. But it means I can't claim that communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
u11:
Amish young people make an adult choice about whether to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. The popular caricature of Rumspringa as a free-for-all that every teenager goes through is exaggerated. But adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If a community's children never leave, it can't know whether they'd come back freely. Let them study, travel and make friends. Let them run into other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
u12: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary families don't hand an eighteen-year-old a pile of money to go explore the world. They try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
u13: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's that leaving shouldn't be made artificially impossible. If children grow up without using money, they especially need to know enough about the money world outside not to be helpless in it: jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID, transportation, and how to ask for help. They need skills and an education they can take with them, relationships outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next path, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community can offer temporary housing, help with travel, tools, or a small reserve for the transition, great. If it can't, it can still avoid punishing anyone for leaving, or holding back the knowledge and the records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing gives perfect freedom. The point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
u14:
Some of them may leave for good. Others may start communities with different values, instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.

Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split over screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Now multiply that by twenty adults with twenty childhoods.

Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once a child is already living inside the disagreement. A community needs enough shared principles about raising children to offer coherence, and enough room left for parents to still be parents.
